title: A helicopter built for five test flights on Mars ended up flying 72 times

cover.alt: NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter standing on four thin legs on reddish Martian ground, with two stacked rotors and a small solar panel on top.

body: Ingenuity rode to Mars with the Perseverance rover, and on 19 April 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight by an aircraft on another world. The Martian air is about **a hundredth as dense** as Earth’s at sea level, so its two 1.21 m rotors had to spin about ten times faster than a helicopter needs on Earth to make enough lift. It was meant as a technology demonstration of only five flights, but it kept going for nearly three years and more than 17 km, until a rotor blade broke off in January 2024.

slides.question: Across all 72 flights, how many minutes in total was Ingenuity in the air?
slides.explanation: 2 hours, 8 minutes and 48 seconds, spread over 1,004 days: under two minutes per flight on average.

slides.label: rotor turns a minute needed to fly in Mars’s thin air
slides.text: Ingenuity weighs about 1.8 kg. Its two rotors spin in opposite directions, one above the other.

slides.alt: Ingenuity seen from a distance on a rocky orange plain, its rotors and solar panel dusty.
slides.caption: Ingenuity on 18 April 2023, photographed by Perseverance’s Mastcam-Z, its rotors and solar panel coated in Martian dust.
slides.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU, processed by Simeon Schmauß · CC BY 2.0

slides.prompt: Ingenuity carried a small tribute to the history of flight. What was it?
slides.answer: A scrap of wing cloth from the 1903 Wright Flyer
slides.detail: It is attached to a cable under the solar panel. NASA named Ingenuity’s first airstrip Wright Brothers Field.
